abstract: Highlights • We establish a novel in vitro microevolution model of M. tuberculosis under capreomycin (Cm) pressure. • Gly232Asp TlyA and Trp120fs TlyA mutations are directly associated with low-level Cm resistance. • Mutations in Ala48Val mmaA2, Gln19Arg rpmA, and variant at the promoter of eis (c.−14c> t ) mediate cross-resistance pathways specific to Cm selection. • Multi-omics (transcriptome/proteome/metabolome) reveals non-genetic resistance mechanisms via lipid metabolism reprogramming and metal ion transport. • Our findings reveal that Cm resistance is a combined effect of both genetic and non-genetic changes, providing potential optimization strategies to the molecular drug sensitivity testing used in clinical practice.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
4.1
Bacterial strains, growth conditions and DNA manipulations
The strains used in this study are listed in Table S1 and Table S2. The bacteria were cultivated as previously described (
Zhao et al., 2019
). The plasmids are listed in Table S3. For the validation of drug-resistance related targets, the genes to be tested were cloned into PKW08 vector using the ClonExpress Ultra One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme, China). The target gene-containing constructs were transformed into C8–7 strain by electroporation. Recombinant strains were cultured in 7H9 medium supplemented with 10 % oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase (OADC) and 50 μg/mL hygromycin B (Sigma-Aldrich) to mid-log phase (OD 600 of 0.8) and induced with 0 or 20 ng/mL tetracycline for 2 days at 37 °C. For determination of promoter activity, the wild and mutated promoters were cloned into pSD5B vector. The recombinant vectors were transformed into
Mycobacterium smegmatis
mc
2
155 (Msm). Recombinant Msm strains were cultured in 7H9 medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin (Sigma-Aldrich) for the subsequent promoter activity assay.
4.2
In vitro induction of Cm-resistant Mtb
The induction of Cm-resistant strains in vitro was carried out according to previously published method with some modifications (
Zhao et al., 2019
). The criteria for Cm-resistant strains set by WHO indicated that Mtb H37Rv strains could not survive when exposed to the critical concentration (CC) of 40.0 mg/L Cm on LJ media. Briefly, the Mtb H37Rv monoclonal strain was chosen as the parental strain (P0) for inducing Cm resistance. P0 strain was cultivated for approximately 4 weeks on LJ medium with a continuous 2-fold gradient of the critical concentration (40 mg/L for Cm), i.e. 2
−4
, 2
−3
, 2
−2
, 2
−1
, 2°-fold of CC. A drug-free culture was used as control. Strains that growing well were collected as the P1 strain. These procedures were repeated until the minimal inhibitory concentration of strains reached the CC (40 mg/L), and the colony morphologies were comparable with that of the drug-free control group. To stabilize the resistant phenotypes, the culture was passaged for 2–3 generations on LJ medium with 40 mg/L Cm. Next, to obtain strains with high levels of Cm resistance, the P10 strains were cultured on LJ medium with 2-, 4-, and 8-fold CC of Cm to the 27 cultural passages, which grew well on 8-fold CC medium. The antimicrobial susceptibility of all the lab-selected strains and clinical isolates were tested using the Sensititre MYCOTB MIC plate (BASO, China) according to manufacturer’s instructions. The 8th and 27th generation strains selected by Cm and the previously reported 3rd generation strains selected by Am (
W Wei et al., 2023
) were incubated on 7H10 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC, and then the appropriate number of single colonies were selected to detect the mutation of tlyA and rrs by targeted sequencing of PCR amplicons. The primers used are listed in Table S3.
4.3
Whole genome resequencing
Mtb genomic DNA was extracted and purified using Bacterial DNA Extraction Kit (Gene-Optimal, China). PCR-free DNA libraries for full-genome sequencing were constructed from the genomic DNA of the selected strains using a TruSeq DNA kit (Illumina, Inc.) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The average insert size of each sample was 350 bp. The libraries were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq or HiSeq 2000 sequencing systems. A base-calling pipeline (version HC1.4/RTA1.12) was used to process raw fluorescent images. The average Q20 rate of the original sequence was 98.0 %. We used FASTP software (V0.20.0) to filter raw data (parameter: FastP-Q20-L50-R-F5-F5). High-quality paired-end reads were mapped to the reference H37Rv genome (GenBank
NC_000962.3
) using BWA MEM v0.7.1231 or Geneious 6.0 (Biomatters Ltd., Auckland, New Zealand). Nucleotide variants including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and short insertions or deletions were called by Snippy (V4.6.0) with default parameters (
https://github.com/tseemann/snippy
).
4.4
RNA-seq analysis
Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were independently cultured to the logarithmic growth phase (an optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.8) in drug-free medium with 3 replicates. Then each strain was divided into 4 aliquots for RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, proteomic analysis and metabolomic analysis, respectively. 50 ml of exponentially growing cultures was harvested by centrifugation and washed twice with PBS buffer. Total RNA was isolated using a total RNA extraction kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The bacterial precipitate was mixed evenly with RNA isolater, then 1/5 vol of chloroform was added and mix vigorously, the mixture was left to stand at 4 °C for 5 min. The samples were centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was carefully collected and mixed with an equal volume of isopropanol. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C for 10 min. The sample was centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The RNA pellet was washed with 75 % ethanol and centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was air-dried at room temperature. The dried pellet was dissolved in nuclease-free water. RNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis, and the purity and concentrations were determined using a spectrophotometer.
The RNA samples were treated with DNase I. The quality and quantity of each sample were assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). For RNA sequencing, the cDNA libraries were prepared using NEBNext UltraTM RNA library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, USA). After ribosomal RNA removal, the qualities were checked with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform. Reads were mapped to H37Rv reference genome using Bowtie2 v2.2.6 with default parameters to generate BAM files. Gene expression values were analyzed based on FPKM with HTSeq v0.6.0. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were determined with DESeq v1.22.1. Genes with a multiple hypothesis-adjusted p-value below 0.05 (adjusted p-value < 0.05) were considered as DEGs. Functional enrichment analysis was carried out using GOseq v1.22 based on the Gene Ontology database. The reliability of the data was assessed based on the quality of the biological replicates, with the evaluation criteria referencing the PCA plot. As illustrated in the figure S6, samples with more similar compositions exhibit closer distances in the PCA plot, indicating superior repeatability. In addition, the correlations of gene expression levels between samples are a critical metric for assessing the reliability of the experiment and the appropriateness of sample selection. The overall qualities of RNA-seq were validated by the Pearson correlation coefficient squared across all biological replicates (Table S11).
4.5
Promoter activity assay
Determination of promoter activity was performed as previously described (
Zhang et al., 2013
). The tested promoter sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S3.
4.6
RT-qPCR
RT-qPCR was performed according to previously published procedures (
W Wei et al., 2023
). The primers used in this study are listed in Table S3.
4.7
Proteomic assay
For total protein extraction, Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were suspended with lysis buffer (PBS (pH 7.4) with 1 mM EDTA, 30 μl DNase, 30 μl RNase, and one Complete EDTA-free protease inhibitor tablet), followed by lysis in a MP Biomedicals Fastprep-24 instrument (speed 6.5, time 30 s) for 5 cycles. Bacteria were incubated on ice for 5 min between each cycle. Samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15–30 min at 4 °C. Subsequently, the supernatant was transferred into a clean tube and filtered twice with a 0.22 μm filter (Millipore). Protein concentration was measured using Micro BCA Protein Assay Kit (Sangon Biotech, China).
To investigate the difference in protein levels of these four strains, we used 12-plex tandem mass tags proteomic assay. Each group included three independent replicates. The detailed procedures and parameters of enzymolysis, labeling, mass spectrometry and bioinformatics analysis were described in the appendix.
4.8
mRNA and protein correlation analysis
To compare the consistency of transcriptomic and proteomic changes after drug treatment at Table S9, we analyzed the correlations between quantitative and differentially expressed genes and proteins in terms of both expression and functional enrichment. Spearman’s correlation tests were performed on transcriptome and proteome.
4.9
Lipid metabolomics analysis
Four representative Mtb strains (8–9 replicates for each strain) were washed twice with 1 ml chromatographic grade pure water, and the supernatant was discarded. The bacteria were suspended with 100 μL pure water, and 800 μL MTBE (Methyl‑tert‑butyl‑ether) was added and mixed by vortex. 240 μL of pre-cooled methanol was added, mixed and transferred to the lysis matrix B tube. Bacteria were disrupted in a MP Biomedicals Fastprep-24 instrument (speed 6.5, time 30 s) for 5 cycles. Cells were incubated on ice for 5 min between each cycle. Finally, the samples were ultrasound in a low-temperature water bath for 20 min, placed at room temperature for 30 min, centrifuged at 12,000 rpm at 4 °C for 15 min. The upper organic phase was harvested and transferred to a fresh glass vial for LC/MS analysis. The quality control (QC) sample was prepared by mixing a 20 μL of the supernatants from all the samples. LC-MS/MS analyses were performed by Biotree Technology (Shanghai, China). The detailed procedures and parameters were described in the appendix.
4.10
Phenotypic analysis of Mtb strains
Four representative Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were used for sliding motility, Congo Red assay, biofilm formation and growth curve measurement. 2 μL culture of each strain (OD600 of 0.8) were dispensed on plate containing 7H9 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC and 0.3 % agar to detect the sliding motility. Another 2 μl culture was dropped on 7H10 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC and 100 μg/ml Congo red (Sigma) to observe Congo red staining and colony morphology. To test the difference in biofilm formation of the strains, 100 μl culture was inoculated in Sauton’s medium.

1
Introduction
The drug-resistant TB, including rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis (RR-TB), multidrug-resistant tuberculosis (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), is a life-threatening infectious disease and has greatly endangered global public health. Capreomycin (Cm) is a macrocyclic peptide antibiotic, which had been used as a major second-line injectable drug (SLID) in the treatment of drug-resistant TB before 2019. A study enrolled over 12,000 patients across 50 MDR-TB cohorts spanning 25 countries has found that the use of kanamycin (Km) and Cm was associated with adverse treatment outcomes and increased mortality (
Cegielski et al., 2021
). On the basis of this evidence from the large cohort study, Km and Cm are no longer recommended for MDR-TB treatments by the World Health Organization (WHO). Currently, only amikacin (Am) is classified into group C in the updated subgroup. It should be noted that the evidence on WHO’s recommendations rarely included the data from Chinese patients. The treatments of drug-resistant TB in China have its own characteristics compared with other countries in terms of drug accessibility, drug resistance spectrum of patient population, and adverse treatment reactions.
More recently, an all-oral regimen has been recommended, leaving behind the injectable anti-TB drugs altogether (
WHO 2022
). The clinical trials of the all-oral regimen are still ongoing and the data on its effectiveness remains limited. However, several preliminary studies have indicated that most patients being considered for new regimens in Haiti and India have developed resistance to the key oral drugs, such as bedaquiline, bringing the practical effectiveness of the all-oral regimen in question (
Walsh et al., 2019
;
Udwadia et al., 2019
). The cost of WHO recommended treatment is not affordable for most TB patients, especially in the economically underdeveloped regions. Under the circumstance of "ideal plan" recommended by WHO, the cost of a complete treatment course is about $14,300 ∼ $24,300, with the bedaquiline provided free of charge through charitable donation projects. Therefore, most of the drugs within group A and B of the updated WHO guidelines, such as bedaquiline, delamanid and pretomanid, have not yet been included in China’s essential drug list and medical insurance reimbursement list because of their high prices. In contrast, most injections, such as Am and Cm, are easily accessible and affordable, with 85 % being reimbursed by medical insurance, and have been widely used in China for many years. Chinese clinicians have amassed substantial expertise in the surveillance and management of adverse reactions associated with second-line injectable anti-tuberculosis medications. Several studies conducted in China have demonstrated that the combination of Cm with quinolone anti-TB drugs, such as levofloxacin and moxifloxacin, can effectively improve the cure rate of MDR-TB (
Zhang et al., 2016
;
Li, 2021
;
Yin et al., 2020
).
Cm interferes with ribosome function and inhibits protein synthesis, but the specific mechanism of action of its antibacterial effects has not been fully clarified. Studies have shown that Cm can bind to the 16S rRNA of Mtb and inhibit its function (
Fu and Shinnick, 2007
). Cm interferes with the ribosome functions in Mtb and hinders protein synthesis by inhibiting the interaction between ribosomal protein L12 and L10 (
Lin et al., 2014
). The resistance mechanism of Cm has been considered to be mainly related to gene mutations, including rrs (Rvnr01) (
Jian et al., 2018
), tlyA (Rv1694) (
Maus et al., 2005
), and eis (Rv2416c) which encodes an N-acetyltransferase (
Chen et al., 2011
). The most common rrs mutation leading to Cm resistance is A1401G (
Kambli et al., 2016
), which also results in cross-resistance to Cm with Am and/or Km. Cm and Am historically shared common resistance pathways, yet recent clinical and genetic data suggest differences. These difference prompts a systematic comparison of the evolutionary trajectories under Cm and Am pressure, which is the focus of this study.
TlyA encodes the 2′-O-methyltransferase and acts by methylation of nucleotide C1409 in 16S rRNA helix 44 and nucleotide C1920 in 23S rRNA helix 69. Loss of methylation due to
tlyA
gene mutations can result in Cm resistance (
Monshupanee et al., 2012
). Thr70Ala and Thr25Ala mutations within the open reading framework of
eis
gene are also related to Cm resistance (
Jnawali et al., 2013
). In addition, several efflux pumps were also reported relative to Cm resistance, such as
Y177H
Rv1258c,
G170V
Rv0194 and
R83G
Rv0194 (
Malinga et al., 2016
). Moreover, the deletion of 23S rRNA rrl A1916 in Mtb and
Escherichia coli
, as well as three mutations of 23S rRNA helical H69 in
Thermus thermophilus
(A1913U, mU1915G △mU1915) also caused Cm resistance (
Johansen et al., 2006
;
Monshupanee et al., 2008
).
Almost all the Cm-resistant mutations are discovered by the genome or target gene sequencing of clinical strains. The clinical strains have complex backgrounds and various mutation types, some of which could be related to lineages (
Oppong et al., 2019
). As a result, it is difficult to determine the causative mutations of Cm resistance. Furthermore, these studies do not explain why patients develop resistance to Cm without receiving Cm anti-TB therapy. Several efforts have been made to study the resistance and virulence of Mtb to Cm by examining the gene expression of Mtb exposed to Cm (
Miryala et al., 2019
). We have reported that tlyA mutation is a major factor causing low-level Cm resistance of Mtb in vitro (
Zhao et al., 2019
).
In this study, using a selection assay by continuous culture through 27 passages with increasing concentrations of Cm, we established a microevolutionary model of Cm-resistant Mtb to reveal how Mtb evolves from sensitivity to resistance and from low-level to high-level resistance. By analyzing the mutations in each generation of selected Mtb strain, we found that in addition to
Gly232Asp
tlyA and
Trp120fs
tlyA directly associated with low-level resistance to Cm, mutations
Ala48Val
mmaA2,
Gln19Arg
rpmA and eis (c.−14c>
t
) were associated with cross-resistance caused by Cm. The integrated transcriptome-proteome-lipid metabolome analysis of representative selected strains showed that cross-resistance of Cm-selected strains was caused by a combination of both genetic and non-genetic factors, which was different from the induction of Am. By systematically characterizing the molecular mechanisms of Cm resistance, we propose that the "genetic factors" (DNA mutations) are often the drivers that induce the stable "non-genetic factors" (dysregulated pathways, such as eis overexpression, metal ion transport, and metabolic reprogramming), which ultimately mediate the resistance phenotype. Our study significantly enhances understanding of the Cm-resistant mechanisms. Importantly, these findings could improve the guidance and rational use of Cm in clinic practice.
2
Result
2.1
A laboratory evolutionary model of Cm-resistant MTB reveal the genetic evolution of co-resistance
2.1.1
Establishment of the microevolution model
To globally study the resistance mechanism of Mtb to Cm, we generated Cm-resistant strains with different resistance levels. We carried out an in vitro evolutionary experiment under selective Cm pressure using the proportion method on Löwenstein-Jensen (LJ) media recommended by WHO. (
Fig. 1
A). The parental wild-type Mtb H37Rv was cultured in parallel without Cm as control. Through the in vitro evolution process, each cultural passage of positive clones was preserved, enabling us to track the genetic adaptation and the drug-resistant phenotypes of Mtb strains under drug pressure. This approach allowed us to analysis the associations between the drug resistance phenotypes and genetic mutations or non-genetic factors.
Fig. 1
Genetic mutations acquired during the evolutionary process associated with Cm resistance.
(A) Schematic diagram of laboratory evolution of Cm-induced Mtb drug resistance. The induced Mtb strains of each generation were preserved and subjected to MIC measurements and downstream experiments. CC, the WHO recommended critical concentration (40 mg/L for Cm). (B) Accumulation of Mtb gene mutations caused by Cm. The number in “Drug stress” represents the corresponding drug concentration in LJ medium during induction. (C) Validation of drug-resistance related genes. The target genes were cloned into PKW08 vector. Recombinant plasmids harboring the target genes were transformed into C8–7 strain by electroporation. The antimicrobial susceptibility of the recombinant strains was tested by the Sensititre MYCOTB MIC plate (BASO, China) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Tc, tetracycline; wt, wild type. (D) The mutations at gene promoters enhance the expression levels of downstream genes. (a) The promoter sequences, with or without the SNPs (eis (c.−14c>
t
) and Rv0807(c.−50
g
>
t
)), were cloned into the pSD5B plasmid. β-
d
-galactosidase activities were measured. Data is shown as mean values ± SEM from independent biological replicates. ** represents P-value < 0.01. (b) Semi-quantitative RT-PCR was used to test the expression of the downstream genes. Data was analyzed using the 2
-ΔΔCT
method with the Mtb gene sigA as the internal control. Data is shown as mean values ± SEM from independent biological replicates. ** represents P value < 0.01. (c) The antimicrobial susceptibility of the eis-overexpressing strain was tested by the Sensititre MYCOTB MIC plate (BASO, China) according to manufacturer’s instructions. Tc, tetracycline; wt, wild type.
Fig 1
The Mtb strain displayed resistance to Cm at the fourth cultural passage (P4) with slower growing rate. Therefore, we continuously cultivated the Mtb to the seventh passage (P7) when the growth rate was comparable to that of the drug-free controls. Next, to study the mechanism by which Mtb adapts resistance to high concentrations of Cm, we continued to give the above-mentioned selected drug-resistant strains with 2-, 4-, and 8-fold of the critical concentration (CC, 40 μg/mL on LJ medium) (
Woods, 2011
), and generated the corresponding Cm-resistant strains at the P15, P20 and P27 passages.
To systematically investigate the drug resistance phenotypes, we examined the MICs of 14 anti-TB drugs and the cross-resistance of the selected Mtb strains (Table S1(a) and (b)). The Mtb strains were resistant to Cm as early as P2. The strains were resistant only to Cm till P8, with the MIC increasing to 8 μg/mL in liquid medium. After the ninth generation, the Mtb strains displayed cross-resistance to Am, Km and Cm, and the corresponding MICs gradually increased (Table S1(a)). Together, we successfully generate an in vitro evolutionary model of Cm-resistant Mtb.
2.1.2
Identification of Cm resistance-associated mutations in the evolved strains
To identify the genetic mutations directly associated with the drug-resistant phenotypes, we performed whole-genome sequencing analysis (WGS) on the lab-evolved strains. Mutations in genes tlyA, plcC, hemA, PPE51, rpmA, mmaA2 and eis were highly enriched (
Fig. 1
B and Table S1(a)). TlyA is a well-known target gene associated with Cm resistance. In line with our previous reports, we identified two mutated forms of gene tlyA, point mutation (Gly232Asp) and deletion mutation (Trp120fs), in the Cm-resistant strains (
Zhao et al., 2019
), validating our evolutionary model as a powerful tool to discover drug-resistant mutations.
Intriguingly, the evolutionary trajectory of the drug-resistant strains showed dynamic mutation patterns. For example, the
Trp120fs
tlyA mutation was adapted from P6 to P23, and dropped-out under increased Cm pressure after P24 (
Fig. 1
B). Additionally, the Mtb strains evolved multiple mutations related to drug-resistance.
Gln462Arg
plcC and two tlyA mutations were initially adapted in strains resistant to low levels Cm. Two mutations, i.e.
His139Arg
hemA and
Ala87Pro
PPE51, were further developed in strains resistant to low levels Am and high levels Cm. Mutations
Gln19Arg
rpmA, eis (c.−14c>
t
) and Rv0807 (c.−50
g
>
t
) were associated with cross-drug resistance and high-level Cm resistance (
Fig. 1
B and Table S1(a)).The drug-resistant mutations were identified from in vitro evolved strains. To contextualize our findings within established resistance markers, we compared the mutations identified in our Cm-selected strains with those listed in the latest WHO TB mutation catalogue (ISBN: 9789240082410). The tlyA p.Gly232Asp variant is listed as ‘Associated with Resistance-Interim’, consistent with our functional validation. Although the tlyA p.Trp120fs mutation identified in our model is not currently included in the WHO catalogue, we found that similar mutation types of this gene have been extensively detected in the WHO list and are classified as 'Associated with Resistance-Interim'. This suggests that tlyA p.Trp120fs might be a novel or relatively uncommon Cm-resistant variant. Among other mutations, the eis promoter variant (c.−14c>
t
) is also recognized by WHO as associated with low-level resistance to aminoglycosides. Mutations in mmaA2, hemA, and plcC were not specifically listed for Cm resistance in the WHO catalogue. To verify if there were variants in these genes in the clinical pathogenic strains in real-world, we performed WGS on three types of clinical isolates from the biobank established at our institution: (1) Am/Km/Cm-susceptible strains (74 strains); (2) mono-Cm resistant Mtb strains (16 strains); (3) cross-resistant strains (67 strains). We identified variants in genes tlyA, eis, hemA, mmaA2 and plcC in the Mtb clinical isolates (Table S2). Due to the limited size of our clinical samples, we did not find any variants in genes rpmA and ppe51. Notably, a previous study has reported putative Am resistance markers in the ppe51 gene from 1184 SLIDs-resistant clinical Mtb strains (
Conkle-Gutierrez et al., 2022
). Together, these results suggest that our in vitro evolutionary model successfully identify drug-resistant mutations in Mtb.
2.1.3
Functional validation of resistance-associated mutations
To determine whether these mutations confer resistance, we individually introduced the mutations into the
Gly232Asp
tlyA strain and examined their drug resistance. The
Gly232Asp
tlyA strain were obtained from the P8 monoclone (C8–7). We expressed both the mutations and the wild-type controls using a tetracycline-inducible system. We subsequently examined the MICs of Cm, Km and Am in the recombination strains using the broth microdilution method. Notably, the heteroploidy strain
Gly232Asp/WT
tlyA was resistant to Cm (MICs≤2 mg/L), suggesting that
Gly232Asp
tlyA is a dominant mutation (Fig. S1). All the heteroploidy strains of tested mutations could elevated the MICs of Am and Km, at or below the resistance threshold (
Fig. 1
C and Fig. S1). To further investigate the impact of the mutations on drug resistance levels, we overexpressed the wild-type and mutant forms of tlyA, rpmA, mmaA2, hemA, PPE51, and the wild-type of eis in the H37Rv strain (Fig. S2). Overexpression of the wild-type eis gene, as well as the tlyA, rpmA, mmaA2, hemA, and PPE51 mutants, enhanced resistance to Km or Cm to varying extents.
In addition to the mutations located in the coding regions, we also identified two IGR mutations within the promoters of eis and Rv0807. The non-coding mutations were isolated from the monoclonal strain C27–1 (Table S1(e)) derived from P27. To study the effects of the mutations on gene transcription, we performed promoter activity assay. The promoter activities with eis (c.−14c>
t
) and Rv0807 (c.−50
g
>
t
) were 14.6-fold and 2.2-fold higher than the wild-type controls, respectively (
P
< 0.05) (
Fig. 1
D(a)). Subsequently, we verified the expression levels of eis and Rv0807 in C27–1 strain by qRT-PCR. Only
eis
levels in the C27–1 strain significantly increased compared to both the control and C8–7 strains (
P
< 0.01) (
Fig. 1
D (b)), suggesting that the mutations increase promoter activities and upregulate the eis expression levels. We wondered if eis upregulation was sufficient to lead to the cross-resistance phenotypes. Therefore, we introduced wild-type
eis
into the C8–7 strain (with
Gly232Asp
tlyA). The heteroploidy strain significantly elevated the MICs of SLIDs (
Fig. 1
D (c)). However, the Km/Am/Cm-resistance level of heteroploidy
WT
eis strain was lower than C27–1 clone, suggesting that the cross-resistance of SLIDs is caused by combinatory mutations.
2.2
Transcriptome analysis described unique transcriptional features to the cm-resistant strains
To further investigate the process and mechanism of high-level Cm resistance in Mtb, we examined the global RNA expression on parental control P0 and two representative lab-selected Cm-resistant Mtb strains, C8–7 (P8) and C27–1 (P27). Genes with a multiple hypothesis-adjusted p-value below 0.05 (adjusted p-value < 0.05) were considered as differentially expressed genes (DEGs) (Table S4). There were 318 DEGs including 210 up-regulated and 108 down-regulated genes between P0 and C8–7 strain, and 490 DEGs including 302 up-regulated and 188 down-regulated genes between P0 and C27–1 (
Fig. 2
A). 187 genes were differentially regulated in both C8–7 and C27–1 (
Fig. 2
B).
Fig. 2
Transcriptional profiles of the representative lab-induced Cm-resistant strains.
(A) Volcano plot of differentially expressed genes (DEGs) between parental strain P0 and Cm-resistant strains. The X axis represents log2-transformed fold change, the Y axis represents -log10-transformed adjusted p-values. The red points represent upregulated DEGs, the green points represent downregulated DEGs, and the blue points represent non-DEGs. (B) Venn diagram represents the numbers of overlapping differentially expressed genes of the two Cm-resistant strains compared to the P0 strain. (C) GO classification of DEGs in strain C27–1. (D) Heatmap of the expression levels of DEGs in Cm-resistant strain/P0 obtained from RNA-seq. (a) The top 34 DEGs. (b) The 15 DEGs within the mce1 and mce4 operons. (E) Individually verifications of the DEGs from RNA-seq in panel (D) by RT-qPCR.
Fig 2
The DEGs of C27–1 were significantly enriched in 31 gene ontology (GO) terms (adjusted p-value < 0.05). The down-regulated genes were enriched in gene expression, macromolecule biosynthetic process, RNA biosynthetic process. Whereas the up-regulated genes were enriched in membrane component (
Fig. 2
C). The GO terms enriched by down-regulated DEGs of C8–7 were similar to those of C27–1, whereas no GO terms were significantly enriched among the up-regulated DEGs of C8–7 (Table S5). Then, we performed KEGG pathway analysis on the subset of these DEGs. Compared with P0 strain, up-regulated genes in C27–1 strain were significantly enriched in ABC transporter (corrected p-Value = 0.0007), while down-regulated genes were significantly enriched in steroid degradation pathway (corrected p-Value =0.01884). In C8–7 strain, the up-regulated genes were enriched in ABC transporter (corrected p-Value = 0.10207) and nitrogen metabolism (corrected p-Value = 0.10207) (Table S6). Notably, in C8–7 strain, five enriched ABC transporters were predominantly members of the mce1 family. Whereas in C27–1 strain, thirteen ABC transporters were primarily located near the mce1 and mce4 operons. The mce1 and mce4 operons encode a group of cell-wall proteins, which are responsible for cholesterol and mycolic acids in Mtb. These proteins are essential for the membrane permeability and survival of Mtb into host cells.
To validate the gene expression changes in the drug-resistant clones, we examined 34 top DEGs using RT-qPCR. Specifically, we picked 15 DEGs regulated by the mce1 and mce4 operons. Consistent with the transcriptome results, we observed similar gene expression changes (
Fig. 2
D,
Fig. 2
E, Table S4). Together, these results suggest that a global gene expression changes lead to drug-resistant phenotypes.
2.3
Integrative analysis of transcriptome and proteome revealed the pathway of cross-resistance caused by Cm
2.3.1
Proteomic analysis of the representative resistant strains
Post-transcriptional regulations of RNA may also affect the protein levels and functions. Therefore, to better understand the evolutionary mechanisms of drug-resistance, we further examined the global protein levels in the drug-resistant clones using Tandem Mass Tags (TMT) method (
Thompson et al., 2003
). We detected 2961 proteins in total. Proteins with peptides ≥ 2, CV < 0.5, a multiple hypothesis-adjusted p-value < 0.05 and fold-change ≥ 1.2 were considered as differentially expressed proteins (DEPs) (Table S7). We identified 622 DEPs in C8–7 strain and 519 DEPs in C27–1 strain compared to the parental control (
Fig. 3
A).

Cm- and Am-selections trigger independent cross-resistance pathways
The tlyA is a major mutation type identified in our Cm evolutionary model. We have previously reported that rrs r.A1401G is a major mutation type in an Am-selected model. The rrs r.A1401G mutation leads to high levels of Am resistance and moderate levels of Cm resistance (
W Wei et al., 2023
). Intriguingly, we did not identify any tlyA mutations in the Am-selected model. This implies that the Am and Cm selected cross-resistance could induce different pathways. To characterize the mechanisms of Am and Cm induced cross-resistance, we utilized a previous reported strain A3–1 strain (Table S1), which had evolved under Am pressure, and analyzed its profiles at the transcriptional, protein and metabolic levels.
In our previous report, 274 genes were differentially regulated (151 downregulated and 123 upregulated) in A3–1 strain compared to the P0 parental strain (Table S4) (
W Wei et al., 2023
). To compare the Am- and Cm-resistant strains, we intersected the DEGs (fold-change ≥ 1.5) in C27–1 and A3–1 strains. 29 genes were differentially regulated under Am or Cm pressure (Fig. S3). 24 out of 29 genes were verified with consistent expression changes using RT-qPCR (Fig. S3). The down-regulated genes in A3–1 strain were enriched in biosynthesis of siderophore group non-ribosomal peptides (corrected P-value =0.027) and TCA cycle (corrected P-value =0.035) pathways (Table S6).
In contrast to the Cm-selected strain C27–1, the integrative analysis of transcriptome and proteome on the A3–1 strain revealed 81 DEPs-DEGs genes, which were significantly enriched in C5-branched dibasic acid metabolism, steroid degradation, tuberculosis and TCA cycle (
Fig. 5
A-C, Table S8). The relative difference of CL, PE, PG and PI were up-regulated in both C27–1 and A3–1 strains (
Fig. 5
D). 34 DELs (fold change > 2 and FDR <0.05) were identified in the A3–1 strain compared to the parental control (
Fig. 5
E). Together, these results suggest that Am- and Cm- resistant strains exhibit distinct characterizations in transcriptome, proteome and lipid metabolism.

Discussion
Capreomycin has traditionally been used in long-term chemotherapy regimens to treat MDR-TB. Although it is not included in the latest WHO recommended drug regimen, in view of various reasons, such as the high price of bedaquiline and local TB resistance, Cm is still an alternative drug for RR-TB and MDR-TB in many developing countries (including China) in the short term. In this study, we established a continuously selected Cm-resistant Mtb model in vitro and systematically revealed Cm-selected drug resistance pathways using multi-omics techniques and functional validation experiments (Fig. S5). Our discoveries improve the understanding the mechanism of action of Cm, providing potential guidance for clinical medication and development of novel drugs for drug-resistant TB.
3.1
The genetic mutation profiles of the cross-resistant strains selected by Cm was distinct with those selected by aminoglycosides
Aminoglycosides (such as Am) and Cm are often classified as functionally similar drugs among anti-TB drugs. In this study, we show that the resistant mechanisms of Mtb to Cm and Am are significantly different. Am-selection induces rrs A1401G mutation leading to cross-resistance of Mtb to the three drugs. However, we did not identify any rrs mutations in our Cm-selected strains. We previously demonstrated a strong correlation between tlyA mutations and Cm resistance (
Zhao et al., 2019
), but resistance was only at low levels of Cm concentrations between 2–4 μg/ml on liquid medium. We speculate that the high-level and cross-drug resistance of Mtb under Cm pressure is gradually accumulated through multiple factors, rather than one single mutation. When exposed to Cm, Mtb will first evolve a pre-resistance state, whose MIC is below the critical threshold of drug resistance and have the tendency to gradually evolve into drug resistance. With continuous subculture and increasing drug concentration, these strains evolved tlyA mutations and acquired low-level Cm resistance. Finally, the accumulation of other mutations, such as plcC, mmaA2, rpmA and eis promoter, gradually increase the drug resistance levels of Mtb strains, and synergistically contribute to the cross-resistance phenotype. It is worth noting that in addition to rpmA, the target genes of the above mutations were also detected in clinical strains, which further indicates that the above mutations have certain clinical significance. mmaA2 has been reported to participate in mycolic acid synthesis by catalyzing the distal cis-cyclopropanation of cis/cis-meromycolates, and its expression is down-regulated under starvation conditions (
Dulberger and Rubin, 2020
). plcC mainly hydrolyzes phospholipids to produce diacylglycerol. Downregulation of mmaA2 could cause drug resistance to ethambutol using a CRISPRi-based functional genomics method (
Li et al., 2022
) . The downregulated rpmA could transiently cause high levels of ethambutol and streptomycin resistance. Ethambutol can inhibit the formation of the mycolic acid-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex on the bacterial cell wall, causing changes in the bacterial wall structure and leading to bacterial death. Therefore, the rpmA and mmaA2 mutations may affect the cell wall structure of Mtb, resulting in cross-resistance.
3.2
The C27–1 strain obtains cross-resistance by inactivating the drug
Our multi-omics data showed that Eis protein was highly expressed in the cross-resistant strain C27–1 (
Fig. 3
E). The eis gene encodes an N-acetyltransferase, which can acetylate Km to inactivate its activity when overexpressed (
Pricer et al., 2012
;
Zaunbrecher et al., 2009
). The eis promoter mutation eis (c.−14c>
t
) has also been shown to cause resistance to Am, just below the critical concentration (
WHO 2021
) . Eis can also cause Cm acetylation to abolish its activity against
Mycobacterium smegmatis
mc
2
155 (
Houghton et al., 2013
). When Eis was overexpressed in C8–7, we observed that the drug resistance levels of the strains to Am, Km and Cm were increased to various degrees (
Fig. 1
D(c)). Therefore, we hypothesize that C27–1 strain caused partial acetylation inactivation of Km and Cm through overexpression of Eis, thereby increasing the resistance level of Mtb to these drugs.
3.3
The C27–1 strain improves its resistance to Cm by regulating the concentration of intracellular metal ions
Cm can act synergistically with metal ions to exert its antibacterial activity. Cm’s nitrogen-rich polypeptide structure enables it to specifically bind with other metal ions, especially copper ions, which is considered as a chelating agent of Cu
2+
(
Stokowa et al., 2012
) . Through the study of Cu
2+
-Cm complex, Cu
2+
can affect the polarity of molecules. Under suitable pH conditions, the antibacterial activity of Cu
2+
-Cm complex group against MTB is 250 times higher than that of pure Cm group (
Manning et al., 2014
). In this study, multi-omics data showed that 8 DEPs-DEGs were enriched in response to metal ions (
Fig. 3
E). Among the upregulated DEPs, ctpH, ctpG, ctpC were P-type ATPases, responsible for excreting metal ions such as copper and zinc from the bacteria to prevent Mtb ion poisoning (
Neyrolles et al., 2013
). Among the 4 down-regulated DEPs, cadI was induced by cadmium, copper and other transition metal, which upregulation might be toxic to mycobacteria (
Ward et al., 2008
); csoR represses the expression of cso (copper sensitive operon) and induces copper in Mtb (
Ward et al., 2008
); KmtR (Rv0827c) is a ArsR/SmtB repressor in Mtb which senses Ni
2+
and Co
2+
and controls expression of a P-type export ATPase (
Riccardi et al., 2008
); Rv3463 had been identified to increase intracellular Ca
2+
in Mtb-infected macrophages. In addition, the upregulated proteins in Rv0097-Rv0101 operons were responsible for biosynthesis of diisonitrile lipopeptide metallophores that facilitate survival under Cu-limiting conditions (
Manning et al., 2014
). Taken together, the C27–1 strain may increase the MIC level of Cm by reducing the level of intracellular copper ions, resulting in a decrease in the formation of Cu
2+
-Cm complexes.
Furthermore, we speculate that the upregulation of metal ion efflux systems (e.g., ctpH, ctpG, ctpC) in C27–1 likely represents an emerging adaptive response to cellular stress induced by the accumulation of multiple resistance mutations. The combinatorial effect of mutations may perturb cellular homeostasis, potentially inducing membrane or oxidative stress. In response, the bacterium may upregulate metal efflux pumps as a compensatory mechanism to alleviate the toxicity of abnormal metal ion accumulation or to reconfigure metal cofactor utilization under stress. This synergy between genetic drivers and physiological adaptations highlights the complexity of high-level resistance evolution. Future studies using combinatorial mutagenesis and stress response assays will be essential for elucidating the exact causal relationships between these mutations and the observed non-genetic adaptations.
3.4
Lipid metabolism is an additional pathway to acquired resistance evolved in C27–1 strains
In this study, transcriptomic analysis of the C27–1 strain revealed that its significantly upregulated gene contained almost complete Mce 1 and Mce 4 operon. The transcriptome-proteome analysis also showed enriching of lipid metabolism-related pathways. Lipid metabolomic results showed total triacylglycerol (TAG) in Cm-selected strains significantly decreased (
Fig. 4
B and
Fig. 4
C), while total TAG in Am-selected strains remained unchanged (
Fig. 5
D and
Fig. 5
E). Host-derived lipids are an important carbon source during Mtb infection and the uptake of major carbon sources in Mtb is accomplished through specialized transporters: Mce1 complex mainly absorbs fatty acids, while Mce4 complex mainly takes up cholesterol (
Mohn et al., 2008
;
Shimono et al., 2003
). Ingested lipids can be converted to TAG for storage in lipid inclusions, or they can be degraded to produce a variety of products, including acetyl-CoA, propionyl-CoA, pyruvate, and possibly succinyl-CoA, which can be used for energy generation or lipid synthesis. TAG can also be used by Mtb as a reservoir of fatty acids required for mycolic acid biosynthesis. It has been shown that TAG in Mtb can be hydrolyzed to provide free even fatty acids for β-oxidation, which in turn provides energy and acetyl-CoA. This acetyl-coA is available for TCA cycle and FAS I type lipid synthesis (
Shi et al., 2010
). A few studies reported the relationship between fatty acid metabolism and drug resistance of Mtb, and most of them focus on drug tolerance (
Goossens et al., 2020
). Several studies have suggested that lipid-induced dormancy state remodels the central carbon metabolism of Mtb and is functionally related to the acquisition of drug resistance (
Xu et al., 2020
;
Aguilar-Ayala et al., 2017
). The transcriptome characteristics of Mtb with cholesterol as the only carbon source showed that cholesterol promotes Mtb enter into a drug-resistant state (
Pawelczyk et al., 2021
). Mtb could reduce its lipid dependence by reducing metabolic activities under INH stress. Mtb upregulates several genes involved in mycolic acid synthesis, which can promote mycolic acid synthesis and bypass INH-induced cell wall damage. In addition, genes involved in lipid metabolism that are indirectly related to the synthesis of mycolic acid are also involved in the stress response induced by INH. For example, TAG synthesis gene tgs1 and genes involved in lipid degradation, such as prpC, fadE24 etc., are upregulated under INH pressure (
Tudó et al., 2010
).
Therefore, we speculated that in addition to gene mutation, Mtb also develops drug resistance by upregulation of Mce1/4 transporter proteins to take in more cholesterol and fatty acids, and regulation of fatty acid synthesis and degradation pathway proteins. On one hand, it provides carbon source and energy for bacteria, so that bacteria maintain low metabolic activities. On the other hand, it changes the lipid structure of the bacterial cell wall, affect the permeability of the cell wall, and contribute to bacterial resistance to drugs. These mechanisms deserve further exploration.
3.5
Clinical implications and future perspectives
It is an effective way to solve the existing problems in a targeted manner by optimizing or reusing old drugs. In recent years, studies have focused on developing Cm as a topical drug, in order to alleviate the problem of toxic side effects and poor patient compliance, such as combining with antimicrobial peptides to make dry powder (
Shao et al., 2021
;
Schoubben et al., 2014
;
Shao et al., 2023
). Compared to intravenous injection, the inhaled Cm showed better pharmacokinetics parameters, such as significantly higher area under the curve, slower clearance and longer mean residence time in both the plasma and lungs. In addition, high local drug concentration could be achieved at the site of primary infection by delivering the Cm directly to the lungs (
Shao et al., 2021
). Therefore, Cm is still an alternative drug under the severe situation of global drug-resistant tuberculosis prevention and control and limited second-line anti-tuberculosis drugs.
In conclusion, using the microevolutionary model of Cm-resistant Mtb, we have revealed how Mtb evolves from sensitive to resistant phenotypes and from low-level to high-level resistance. Unlike Am, which induces rrs A1401G mutation and leads to cross-resistance of Mtb to Am, Km and Cm, Cm does not cause rrs mutations. Cross-resistance selected by Cm is associated with the accumulation of multiple gene mutations, including tlyA, plcC, mmaA2, rpmA and eis promoter. In addition to mutations, the transcriptome-proteome-lipid metabolome analysis showed that acetylating drugs to inactivate their activities, reducing the synergistic effect of Cm and metal ions, and regulating lipid metabolism were also the causes of cross-drug resistance. Numerous studies have revealed that these pathways influence bacterial virulence. Next, the specific relationship between the above identified pathways and drug resistance needs further experimental verification. The relationship between drug resistance and virulence of Mtb should also be of concern. In the short term, Cm is beneficial in the RR-TB/MDR-TB chemotherapy regimen in developing countries. Taking into account systemic administration of Cm (muscular or intravenous route), toxic side effects, and poor patient compliance, topical drugs such as Cm dry powder have a good development prospect. Further research on the resistance mechanism of Cm is helpful to guide clinical drug use and better treat drug-resistant tuberculosis.

MATERIALS AND METHODS
4.1
Bacterial strains, growth conditions and DNA manipulations
The strains used in this study are listed in Table S1 and Table S2. The bacteria were cultivated as previously described (
Zhao et al., 2019
). The plasmids are listed in Table S3. For the validation of drug-resistance related targets, the genes to be tested were cloned into PKW08 vector using the ClonExpress Ultra One Step Cloning Kit (Vazyme, China). The target gene-containing constructs were transformed into C8–7 strain by electroporation. Recombinant strains were cultured in 7H9 medium supplemented with 10 % oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase (OADC) and 50 μg/mL hygromycin B (Sigma-Aldrich) to mid-log phase (OD 600 of 0.8) and induced with 0 or 20 ng/mL tetracycline for 2 days at 37 °C. For determination of promoter activity, the wild and mutated promoters were cloned into pSD5B vector. The recombinant vectors were transformed into
Mycobacterium smegmatis
mc
2
155 (Msm). Recombinant Msm strains were cultured in 7H9 medium supplemented with 50 μg/mL kanamycin (Sigma-Aldrich) for the subsequent promoter activity assay.
4.2
In vitro induction of Cm-resistant Mtb
The induction of Cm-resistant strains in vitro was carried out according to previously published method with some modifications (
Zhao et al., 2019
). The criteria for Cm-resistant strains set by WHO indicated that Mtb H37Rv strains could not survive when exposed to the critical concentration (CC) of 40.0 mg/L Cm on LJ media. Briefly, the Mtb H37Rv monoclonal strain was chosen as the parental strain (P0) for inducing Cm resistance. P0 strain was cultivated for approximately 4 weeks on LJ medium with a continuous 2-fold gradient of the critical concentration (40 mg/L for Cm), i.e. 2
−4
, 2
−3
, 2
−2
, 2
−1
, 2°-fold of CC. A drug-free culture was used as control. Strains that growing well were collected as the P1 strain. These procedures were repeated until the minimal inhibitory concentration of strains reached the CC (40 mg/L), and the colony morphologies were comparable with that of the drug-free control group. To stabilize the resistant phenotypes, the culture was passaged for 2–3 generations on LJ medium with 40 mg/L Cm. Next, to obtain strains with high levels of Cm resistance, the P10 strains were cultured on LJ medium with 2-, 4-, and 8-fold CC of Cm to the 27 cultural passages, which grew well on 8-fold CC medium. The antimicrobial susceptibility of all the lab-selected strains and clinical isolates were tested using the Sensititre MYCOTB MIC plate (BASO, China) according to manufacturer’s instructions. The 8th and 27th generation strains selected by Cm and the previously reported 3rd generation strains selected by Am (
W Wei et al., 2023
) were incubated on 7H10 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC, and then the appropriate number of single colonies were selected to detect the mutation of tlyA and rrs by targeted sequencing of PCR amplicons. The primers used are listed in Table S3.
4.3
Whole genome resequencing
Mtb genomic DNA was extracted and purified using Bacterial DNA Extraction Kit (Gene-Optimal, China). PCR-free DNA libraries for full-genome sequencing were constructed from the genomic DNA of the selected strains using a TruSeq DNA kit (Illumina, Inc.) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. The average insert size of each sample was 350 bp. The libraries were sequenced on the Illumina MiSeq or HiSeq 2000 sequencing systems. A base-calling pipeline (version HC1.4/RTA1.12) was used to process raw fluorescent images. The average Q20 rate of the original sequence was 98.0 %. We used FASTP software (V0.20.0) to filter raw data (parameter: FastP-Q20-L50-R-F5-F5). High-quality paired-end reads were mapped to the reference H37Rv genome (GenBank
NC_000962.3
) using BWA MEM v0.7.1231 or Geneious 6.0 (Biomatters Ltd., Auckland, New Zealand). Nucleotide variants including single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and short insertions or deletions were called by Snippy (V4.6.0) with default parameters (
https://github.com/tseemann/snippy
).
4.4
RNA-seq analysis
Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were independently cultured to the logarithmic growth phase (an optical density at 600 nm (OD600) of 0.8) in drug-free medium with 3 replicates. Then each strain was divided into 4 aliquots for RNA-seq, RT-qPCR, proteomic analysis and metabolomic analysis, respectively. 50 ml of exponentially growing cultures was harvested by centrifugation and washed twice with PBS buffer. Total RNA was isolated using a total RNA extraction kit (Vazyme, Nanjing, China). The bacterial precipitate was mixed evenly with RNA isolater, then 1/5 vol of chloroform was added and mix vigorously, the mixture was left to stand at 4 °C for 5 min. The samples were centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 15 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was carefully collected and mixed with an equal volume of isopropanol. The mixture was incubated at 4 °C for 10 min. The sample was centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 10 min at 4 °C. The RNA pellet was washed with 75 % ethanol and centrifuged at 11,200 rpm for 5 min at 4 °C. The supernatant was discarded, and the pellet was air-dried at room temperature. The dried pellet was dissolved in nuclease-free water. RNA integrity was assessed by agarose gel electrophoresis, and the purity and concentrations were determined using a spectrophotometer.
The RNA samples were treated with DNase I. The quality and quantity of each sample were assessed using an Agilent 2100 Bioanalyzer (Agilent Technologies, USA). For RNA sequencing, the cDNA libraries were prepared using NEBNext UltraTM RNA library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs, USA). After ribosomal RNA removal, the qualities were checked with the Agilent Bioanalyzer 2100 system. Sequencing was performed on the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform. Reads were mapped to H37Rv reference genome using Bowtie2 v2.2.6 with default parameters to generate BAM files. Gene expression values were analyzed based on FPKM with HTSeq v0.6.0. Differentially expressed genes (DEGs) were determined with DESeq v1.22.1. Genes with a multiple hypothesis-adjusted p-value below 0.05 (adjusted p-value < 0.05) were considered as DEGs. Functional enrichment analysis was carried out using GOseq v1.22 based on the Gene Ontology database. The reliability of the data was assessed based on the quality of the biological replicates, with the evaluation criteria referencing the PCA plot. As illustrated in the figure S6, samples with more similar compositions exhibit closer distances in the PCA plot, indicating superior repeatability. In addition, the correlations of gene expression levels between samples are a critical metric for assessing the reliability of the experiment and the appropriateness of sample selection. The overall qualities of RNA-seq were validated by the Pearson correlation coefficient squared across all biological replicates (Table S11).
4.5
Promoter activity assay
Determination of promoter activity was performed as previously described (
Zhang et al., 2013
). The tested promoter sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S3.
4.6
RT-qPCR
RT-qPCR was performed according to previously published procedures (
W Wei et al., 2023
). The primers used in this study are listed in Table S3.
4.7
Proteomic assay
For total protein extraction, Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were suspended with lysis buffer (PBS (pH 7.4) with 1 mM EDTA, 30 μl DNase, 30 μl RNase, and one Complete EDTA-free protease inhibitor tablet), followed by lysis in a MP Biomedicals Fastprep-24 instrument (speed 6.5, time 30 s) for 5 cycles. Bacteria were incubated on ice for 5 min between each cycle. Samples were then centrifuged at 12,000 rpm for 15–30 min at 4 °C. Subsequently, the supernatant was transferred into a clean tube and filtered twice with a 0.22 μm filter (Millipore). Protein concentration was measured using Micro BCA Protein Assay Kit (Sangon Biotech, China).
To investigate the difference in protein levels of these four strains, we used 12-plex tandem mass tags proteomic assay. Each group included three independent replicates. The detailed procedures and parameters of enzymolysis, labeling, mass spectrometry and bioinformatics analysis were described in the appendix.
4.8
mRNA and protein correlation analysis
To compare the consistency of transcriptomic and proteomic changes after drug treatment at Table S9, we analyzed the correlations between quantitative and differentially expressed genes and proteins in terms of both expression and functional enrichment. Spearman’s correlation tests were performed on transcriptome and proteome.
4.9
Lipid metabolomics analysis
Four representative Mtb strains (8–9 replicates for each strain) were washed twice with 1 ml chromatographic grade pure water, and the supernatant was discarded. The bacteria were suspended with 100 μL pure water, and 800 μL MTBE (Methyl‑tert‑butyl‑ether) was added and mixed by vortex. 240 μL of pre-cooled methanol was added, mixed and transferred to the lysis matrix B tube. Bacteria were disrupted in a MP Biomedicals Fastprep-24 instrument (speed 6.5, time 30 s) for 5 cycles. Cells were incubated on ice for 5 min between each cycle. Finally, the samples were ultrasound in a low-temperature water bath for 20 min, placed at room temperature for 30 min, centrifuged at 12,000 rpm at 4 °C for 15 min. The upper organic phase was harvested and transferred to a fresh glass vial for LC/MS analysis. The quality control (QC) sample was prepared by mixing a 20 μL of the supernatants from all the samples. LC-MS/MS analyses were performed by Biotree Technology (Shanghai, China). The detailed procedures and parameters were described in the appendix.
4.10
Phenotypic analysis of Mtb strains
Four representative Mtb strains (P0, C8–7, C27–1 and A3–1) were used for sliding motility, Congo Red assay, biofilm formation and growth curve measurement. 2 μL culture of each strain (OD600 of 0.8) were dispensed on plate containing 7H9 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC and 0.3 % agar to detect the sliding motility. Another 2 μl culture was dropped on 7H10 medium supplemented with 10 % OADC and 100 μg/ml Congo red (Sigma) to observe Congo red staining and colony morphology. To test the difference in biofilm formation of the strains, 100 μl culture was inoculated in Sauton’s medium.
